Senses.Explanation: A “small convocation” is a named communal address, often held in the evening or for a special occasion, whose procedure and content are less fixed than an ordinary hall address. Records then mark small convocations for year-end, opening or closing a retreat, memorial instruction, ordination, and ordinary evening teaching. Senses.Explanation: Dahui directly defines dull sinking by contrast: forgetting and falling into a dark cave is called dull sinking, while deliberate mental succession is called agitation. Literally, dim or dull sinking. Dahui supplies the corpus's clearest direct description: forgetting or blanking out falls into the ghost cave beneath Black Mountain, and the teachings call this dull sinking; he contrasts it with deliberate attention, whose thought-consciousness flies about and is called agitation. Other records label dull sinking “not good” beside “binding thought strays from the real” and pair it repeatedly with agitation as the two named conditions found in the Chan hall. The Chan record also bends the inherited fault-category against simple rejection: Gaofeng says the four graphs “dull sinking and agitation” are themselves buddha-nature, Daodu calls the pair one's place for establishing life, and Dahui tells Lü Juren that whether dull-sunk or agitated, it is still only Lü Juren. The deviation lies in this combination of exact diagnosis, fixed pairing, and masters' refusal to locate the named condition outside the person who reports it.

Senses.Explanation: To pass the barrier is to get through a tested obstruction: the records contrast those already through with those still stopped, and extend the phrase to a barrier-passing eye and phrase. Huanglong Huinan distinguishes the two conditions: 'one already past the barrier swings his arms and goes straight on' (已過關者掉臂徑去), whereas 'this is one who has not passed the barrier' (此未透關者也). Zhongfeng Mingben records a corrective contrast: people thread all old and new public cases onto one string and call it 'passing the barrier' (謂之透關), while 'the tight barrier of life and death beneath their heels has not actually been passed' (脚跟下一座生死牢關，政好不曾透得). The phrase also builds 'an eye that passes the barrier' (透關眼). Yuanwu Keqin asks whether anyone present has such an eye. Chijue Daochong says, 'Passing the barrier requires a barrier-passing eye; obtaining treasure requires one who can distinguish treasure' (透關須具透關眼，得寶須還別寶人). Poshan Haiming answers the question 'What is a phrase that passes the barrier?' (如何是透關句), and Dabian Xianquan contrasts 'one already through the barrier' (已透關者) with 'one not through the barrier' (未透關者). These are recorded descriptions, corrections, and compounds; this entry adds no unrecorded destination beyond the barrier.
